§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Examples include, but are not limited to: An auger, drill, magnet, pile-driver, and boom-attached personnel platform. Audible signal means a signal made by a distinct sound or series of sounds. Examples include, but are not limited to, sounds made by a bell, horn, or whistle. Blocking (also referred to as “cribbing”) is wood or other material used to support equipment or a component and distribute loads to the ground. It is typically used to support lattice boom sections during assembly/disassembly and under outrigger and stabilizer floats.”

§1926.1403 Assembly/Disassembly—selection of manufacturer or employer procedures For assembly or disassembly of equipment or attachments, the employer has a fixed duty and a choice. The fixed duty is to comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1403]. The choice is which procedures to comply with. The employer must use either the manufacturer procedures or its own [29cfr1926.1403].

The first option is the "Manufacturer procedures applicable to assembly and disassembly" [29cfr1926.1403(a)]. The second is employer procedures for assembly and disassembly [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. That second option is conditional: employer procedures may be used "only where the employer can demonstrate" that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406 [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. In deciding between the two, keep in mind that the prohibitions duty is stated separately from the choice of procedures, so selecting employer procedures leaves applicable manufacturer prohibitions in force [29cfr1926.1403].

Synthetic slings affect this decision. According to the note, when an employer uses synthetic slings during assembly or disassembly rigging, the employer must follow manufacturer procedures [29cfr1926.1403-note-1]. The note refers to § 1926.1404(r) [29cfr1926.1403-note-1]. This section does not set out the contents of either § 1926.1406 or § 1926.1404(r). “§ 1926.1403 Assembly/Disassembly—selection of manufacturer or employer procedures. When assembling or disassembling equipment (or attachments), the employer must comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions and must comply with either: (a) Manufacturer procedures applicable to assembly and disassembly, or (b) Employer procedures for assembly and disassembly. Employer procedures may be used only where the employer can demonstrate that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406.” §1926.1405 Disassembly—additional requirements for dismantling of booms and jibs (applies to both the use of manufacturer procedures and employer procedures) These additional disassembly requirements cover dismantling booms and jibs, including dismantling to change their length. They apply under both manufacturer procedures and employer procedures [29cfr1926.1405]. Each restriction covers removing a pin "partly or completely", so before moving any pin, the questions are where it is and how the boom is held.

With the pendants in tension, no pins in the pendants may be removed [29cfr1926.1405(a)]. In that same condition, no top or bottom pins may be removed on boom sections located between the pendant attachment points and the crane or derrick body [29cfr1926.1405(b)].

When the boom is supported by its uppermost section resting on the ground or other support, the restriction covers top and bottom pins on sections between that uppermost section and the crane or derrick body [29cfr1926.1405(c)].

For the cantilevered portion of the boom being removed, meaning the portion ahead of the pendant attachment points, no top pins on its boom sections may be removed "until the cantilevered section to be removed is fully supported" [29cfr1926.1405(d)]. This paragraph names top pins only, while (b) and (c) name both top and bottom pins. “§ 1926.1405 Disassembly—additional requirements for dismantling of booms and jibs (applies to both the use of manufacturer procedures and employer procedures). Dismantling (including dismantling for changing the length of) booms and jibs. (a) None of the pins in the pendants are to be removed (partly or completely) when the pendants are in tension. (b) None of the pins (top or bottom) on boom sections located between the pendant attachment points and the crane/derrick body are to be removed (partly or completely) when the pendants are in tension.”

Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926 Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926—Assembly/Disassembly: Sample Procedures for Minimizing the Risk of Unintended Dangerous Boom Movement For pin removal, the appendix cites § 1926.1404(f)(1): employees must not be under the boom, jib, or other components unless § 1926.1404(f)(2) is met. That exception applies when the employer demonstrates that site constraints require one or more employees to be there. The A/D director must then implement procedures that "minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure under the boom" [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

In the sample, aboveground piping prevents lowering the boom, and the aerial lift, based on the near side, cannot be repositioned, so its basket must go under the boom. A rigged assist crane supports the detaching section, with particular care that the end near the pin removers is well supported. Far side pins come out first, the basket returns to the near side as soon as possible, then near side pins come out [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

During assembly/disassembly, the load's center of gravity must be identified if the stability method requires it. With insufficient information, measures must prevent unintended dangerous movement from misidentifying it. In the sample, the director cannot determine the pick point above a non-symmetrical top section's center of gravity. With personnel clear, it is raised a few inches to check for tipping. If it tips, the hoist line is repositioned and the test repeated until the director determines it can be moved without dangerous movement [29cfr1926.cc.appB]. “2. Section 1926.1404(h)(6)(i) provides that, during assembly/disassembly, the center of gravity of the load must be identified if that is necessary for the method used for maintaining stability. Section 1926.1404(h)(6)(ii) states that, where there is insufficient information to accurately identify the center of gravity, measures designed to prevent unintended dangerous movement resulting from an inaccurate identification of the center of gravity must be used.”

Backward stability before swinging the upperworks, travel, and when attaching or removing equipment components.” §1926.1435(b)(4)(ii) Loss of backward stability “(ii) Loss of backward stability. Backward stability before swinging self erecting cranes or cranes on traveling or static undercarriages.” §1926.1404 Assembly/Disassembly—general requirements (applies to all assembly and disassembly operations) Assembly/disassembly is directed by the A/D director: a competent and qualified person, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons. A lone worker must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. The director must understand the procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)], reviewing them immediately beforehand unless already understanding and having applied them to the same equipment type and configuration [29cfr1926.1404(c)]. Crew must understand tasks, hazards and locations to avoid before work, task changes or additions of personnel [29cfr1926.1404(d)].

Crew must notify you before entering covered out-of-view locations where equipment or load movement could injure them [29cfr1926.1404(e)(1)]. If you know someone went there, move no part or load until the pre-arranged communication system confirms they are safe [29cfr1926.1404(e)(2)]. Nobody may be under components during pin removal unless the employer demonstrates site constraints require it; the director must then minimize movement risk and exposure [29cfr1926.1404(f)].

Rated capacity limits apply in all phases [29cfr1926.1404(g)]. The director addresses ground, blocking, assist crane loads (verified beforehand), pick points, center of gravity, stability at pin removal, snagging, counterweights, backward stability and weather [29cfr1926.1404(h)]. Test the boom hoist brake each time before relying on it; if insufficient, use another specified protection against boom movement [29cfr1926.1404(h)(10)].

Observe manufacturer cantilever limits, or if unavailable, a registered professional engineer's written limit [29cfr1926.1404(j)]. Keep component weights readily available [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Components and configuration affecting capacity or safety follow manufacturer requirements (or written engineer approval if unavailable) or qualifying approved modifications; inspect after assembly [29cfr1926.1404(m)]. Remove and safely stow reusable shipping hardware [29cfr1926.1404(o)]. No jib during pile driving [29cfr1926.1404(p)].

Whenever outriggers or stabilizers are required or used, rules cover extension, floats, visibility and blocking; outriggers, except on locomotive cranes, must take equipment weight off wheels. Locomotive cranes have manufacturer-procedure rules [29cfr1926.1404(q)]. Rigging requires a qualified rigger, synthetic sling protection and compliance with sling manufacturer instructions and recommendations, alongside other applicable rigging standards [29cfr1926.1404(r)]. “If it is not sufficient, a boom hoist pawl, other locking device/back-up braking device, or another method of preventing dangerous movement of the boom (such as blocking or using an assist crane) from a boom hoist brake failure must be used. (11) Loss of backward stability. Backward stability before swinging the upperworks, travel, and when attaching or removing equipment components.”

Assembly/disassembly is directed by the A/D director: a competent and qualified person, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons. A lone worker must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. The director must understand the procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)], reviewing them immediately beforehand unless already understanding and having applied them to the same equipment type and configuration [29cfr1926.1404(c)]. Crew must understand tasks, hazards and locations to avoid before work, task changes or additions of personnel [29cfr1926.1404(d)].

Crew must notify you before entering covered out-of-view locations where equipment or load movement could injure them [29cfr1926.1404(e)(1)]. If you know someone went there, move no part or load until the pre-arranged communication system confirms they are safe [29cfr1926.1404(e)(2)]. Nobody may be under components during pin removal unless the employer demonstrates site constraints require it; the director must then minimize movement risk and exposure [29cfr1926.1404(f)].

Rated capacity limits apply in all phases [29cfr1926.1404(g)]. The director addresses ground, blocking, assist crane loads (verified beforehand), pick points, center of gravity, stability at pin removal, snagging, counterweights, backward stability and weather [29cfr1926.1404(h)]. Test the boom hoist brake each time before relying on it; if insufficient, use another specified protection against boom movement [29cfr1926.1404(h)(10)].

Observe manufacturer cantilever limits, or if unavailable, a registered professional engineer's written limit [29cfr1926.1404(j)]. Keep component weights readily available [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Rigging requires a qualified rigger, synthetic sling protection and compliance with sling manufacturer instructions and recommendations, alongside other applicable rigging standards [29cfr1926.1404(r)].

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “It is typically used to support lattice boom sections during assembly/disassembly and under outrigger and stabilizer floats. Boatswain's chair means a single-point adjustable suspension scaffold consisting of a seat or sling (which may be incorporated into a full body harness) designed to support one employee in a sitting position. Bogie means “travel bogie,” which is defined below. Boom (equipment other than tower crane) means an inclined spar, strut, or other long structural member which supports the upper hoisting tackle on a crane or derrick.”
